repondus.texte: The seed is in the pods, not the flowers, so a spent bloom picked in June has nothing in it yet. Leave those plants where they are until fall, then collect pods once they start splitting open on their own. Scattering that seed on bare ground in October and covering it lightly is exactly the right method: winter gives it the cold spell it needs, and you get seedlings in spring without lifting a finger.

They will. Ours are not stratified, and they need about 30 days of cold before they germinate, so the fridge is where they want to be anyway: sealed bag, cool and dark, until you are a month out from sowing. If you would rather skip the bookkeeping, put them in the ground this fall and let winter do the same job.

Yes to both. Wait until the pods crack open on their own, take the seed you want and let the rest fly; that is how the plant does it anyway. One thing worth knowing: milkweed seed needs roughly a month of cold before it will germinate, and a mild coastal winter does not always deliver that, so a sealed bag in the fridge for 30 days before spring sowing is good insurance. Expect leaves the first year and flowers the second.

Thank you. Yes, the range keeps growing. We would rather not name dates before something is genuinely ready, so the site is the honest picture of what exists today, and the newsletter is where new things get announced first.

Gloves are in development. No launch date to give you, and we would rather not invent one before it is real. The newsletter is where it gets announced first, and lasclay.com shows what is actually available today.

Central Minnesota is good milkweed country. Common milkweed (syriaca) will thrive there, though it spreads by rhizome, so give it a spot where that is welcome. Butterfly weed (tuberosa) and swamp milkweed (incarnata) stay where you put them and suit a garden bed better, tuberosa in dry sun, incarnata anywhere that holds moisture. All eleven species we carry are North American natives, and none of them is tropical milkweed.

Worth answering precisely. The milkweed is grown in Quebec and the insulation is processed at our workshop in Limoilou, Quebec City. Since July, the textile assembly of most finished products happens abroad, mostly in Tunisia. We would rather say that plainly than stretch the word local: the insulating core is ours and made here, the sewing of the shell largely is not.

Good question, and the timing is the whole answer. The floss sits inside the pods, which form after flowering and are harvested in the fall, once the monarchs have already left. The leaves are what the caterpillars eat, and those are never touched. The seed goes back out in packets, so the plant keeps spreading rather than shrinking. 🦋

The garden section of lasclay.com is the live answer: whatever shows as available there is what we actually have on hand. If the one you want is out, the newsletter is the way to hear when it comes back. We would rather not promise a restock date we cannot keep.

Honest answer: there is no official temperature rating on them, and we are not going to invent one. What we can tell you is why the fibre works. Each strand is hollow, so the insulating air sits inside the fibre rather than between fibres, which is also why it keeps insulating when squashed inside a mitten. Customers report wearing them down to around -30 C. Whether that is enough for your hands is a question only you can answer, and worth keeping in mind before you order.

There is an easier route for next time: sow outdoors in the fall and let winter handle the cold stratification for you, no indoor setup and no calendar to keep track of. If you would rather start them inside again, the seed wants about 30 days in the fridge first.

On price, the site carries the current figures and we would rather not talk numbers in a comment thread. On the other half of that, though: milkweed is not actually difficult from seed, it just has one requirement almost nobody mentions. Ours are not stratified, so the seed needs roughly 30 days of cold before it will germinate. Skip that and germination is dismal, which is where most of the reputation comes from. Sow in the fall and winter does the job for you, or give them a month in the fridge before a spring sowing.

Encouraging, and worth holding lightly: monarch counts swing hard from one year to the next, and one good season is not yet a trend. The figure that decides the long run is how much milkweed is standing on the breeding grounds. Flockhart and colleagues put that loss ahead of both climate and deforestation in Mexico as the driver of the decline, which is the whole reason we are trying to make the plant worth growing.

Twelve plants and a thousand seeds is a good position to be in. Two things worth knowing before you sow. Monarchs find a clump far more readily than the same plants scattered around a yard, so putting the new seed in as a patch will do more than the raw count suggests. And stored seed needs roughly 30 days of cold before it germinates, so either sow this fall and let winter do it, or give it a month in the fridge ahead of spring.

Maryland is easy country for this. The deciding factor is usually the spot rather than the state: ground that stays damp favours swamp milkweed (incarnata), a dry sunny bed favours butterfly weed (tuberosa), and common milkweed (syriaca) will take almost anything but travels underground, so it belongs somewhere you do not mind it spreading. None of the eleven species we carry is tropical milkweed. Before ordering, a Maryland native plant list is the better authority on what belongs in your county.

Yes. All eleven species we carry do well from roughly zone 3 through 9, so 8b sits comfortably inside that. Worth clearing up a common confusion while we are here: the zone on a seed packet is the coldest winter the plant will tolerate, not a ceiling. Being warmer than the listed zone is not the problem people assume it is.

Monarch Drive is a fitting address for this. Rocky and poor is closer to ideal than you would think: butterfly weed (tuberosa) sends down a deep taproot and does its best work in lean, well drained ground, the sort that frustrates most garden plants. It sulks in rich soil and hates wet feet, so a rough yard plays to its strengths. Full sun, then leave it alone once established. An Arkansas native plant list is worth a look too, so you know what already belongs on your street.

All eleven species we carry are North American natives, and none of them is tropical milkweed. For Missouri, the usual starting points are common milkweed (syriaca), butterfly weed (tuberosa) and swamp milkweed (incarnata): the first spreads by rhizome and suits an open or naturalized spot, the other two stay where you put them and behave in a garden bed. Worth checking a Missouri native plant list before ordering, since a local range map is more precise than anything we can tell you from here.

Started plants come and go with the season, so the garden section of lasclay.com is the only reliable answer on any given day. If seed is an option for you instead, keep in mind it wants about 30 days of cold before it will germinate, which is why an autumn sowing often turns out simpler than chasing started plants in spring.

Zone 7 is not the limiting factor, all eleven of ours sit comfortably inside that range. Your ground is the real question. Central Arkansas has room for several: swamp milkweed (incarnata) if you have a low or damp corner, whorled milkweed (verticillata) if you want something slender that takes dry ground and stays put, and common milkweed (syriaca) where you have space you are content to see it colonise. Your county extension office will have the documented list for your exact area.

Fair call, and better that you checked than sowed it blind. All eleven species we sell are native to North America and none of them is tropical milkweed, but native to the continent is not the same thing as native to your county, and that distinction matters more than most seed packets let on. Where our species are not right for a region, the honest answer is a local native nursery rather than us.

Agreed on the principle, and the scale is the whole point. Roadsides, utility corridors and unused public ground add up to a great many hectares currently growing nothing much. Flockhart and colleagues traced the decline mainly to milkweed lost across the breeding range, ahead of climate and ahead of what happens at the Mexican overwintering sites. Gardens count, but that sort of land operates at a different order of magnitude.

Stripped milkweed is the good sign rather than the bad one. That is the caterpillars doing precisely what the plant is there for, and being a native perennial it comes back from the roots each spring, often stronger than the year before. Sounds like your garden is already doing the work.
